Pedestrians must not loiter, wait or stage goods on crossings, and must not cross behind reversing trucks or between a truck and its load.

6. Forklift operators and all MHE drivers must give way to pedestrians at every marked crossing, pedestrian zone and dock ramp, reduce to 5 km/h and be prepared to stop. Inside the building the 10 km/h limit and in the fenced yard the 12 km/h limit always drop to 5 km/h wherever people and trucks meet. Operators must sound the horn when approaching blind corners, rack ends and ramp entries and must not overtake or queue across a crossing.

7. Drivers called forward from the marked waiting area to Doors 1-4 inbound or Doors 5-8 outbound who leave the cab must use only the 1.2 m walkways and marked crossings to move between cab and trailer. Drivers must not enter the hall, walk in transport aisles, wait on ramps or levellers, or walk behind other vehicles. They must remain within the walkway system and return to the cab or waiting area when not at their door.

8. Pedestrian routes, gates and sightlines must be kept clear and visible at all times. No pallets, totes, empty pallet stacks, film, waste, chargers or idle hand pallet jacks may be placed on or over the 1.2 m walkways, against barriers, or in front of crossing markings. Loads in adjacent aisles must not overhang the barrier line, and forklift operators must travel with forks low, load stable and forward view unobstructed.

9. Non-compliance with PR-11 — missing vest or S3 footwear, walking outside barriers, crossing outside marked crossings, barrier abuse or speed breach — is stopped immediately by the shift supervisor, corrected and logged for review. Open defects to barriers, markings or signage and any pedestrian near-miss or contact are recorded under PR-11 and PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover and handed over to the incoming supervisor before work restarts.

title: Electric Fleet
text:
### ops.ch09.s1 Electric Fleet

1. Harborwick 3PL operates an all-electric materials handling fleet. No internal-combustion trucks, gas or diesel forklifts are permitted on site at any time. All mechanised handling inside the hall and at the docks is carried out with electric counterbalance forklifts, electric reach trucks and electric pallet jacks, supported by hand pallet jacks for small moves.

2. The powered fleet consists of 9 counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t and 5 reach trucks rated at 2.0 t. The 9 counterbalance trucks carry out general work: unloading support in Zone A, block-stack placement in Zone B, movement to Zone C and movement of wrapped pallets in Zone D. The 5 reach trucks work exclusively in the high-bay racking in Zone B for put-away and retrieval.

3. The site limit of 900 kg per pallet, load included, is well within both truck ratings. A 3.0 t counterbalance forklift may lift any compliant pallet on site at ground and low levels, and a 2.0 t reach truck may lift any compliant pallet at height in the high bays. No pallet over 900 kg may be handled, and no truck may be used to exceed its rated capacity or to lift two pallets as a single load.

4. Rack-bay capacity in Zone B is fixed at 2,700 kg per bay. Truck rating does not override rack rating. Even with a 3.0 t counterbalance or 2.0 t reach truck, a bay must never be loaded beyond 2,700 kg total. In practice this means at most three full-weight pallets at 900 kg each per bay; any load plan that would exceed 2,700 kg in a single bay must be re-allocated before put-away.

5. Low-level movement is supported by 11 electric pallet jacks and 12 hand pallet jacks. Electric pallet jacks are used by inbound operators in Zone A, by forklift operators for ground-level shuttles, and in Zone D for staging lanes, all within the 900 kg pallet limit. Hand pallet jacks are for short, low-level moves by trained staff where powered trucks are not required. Neither type is used for high-bay racking or for stacking above floor level.

6. All pallet handling equipment on site is therefore accounted for as 9 counterbalance forklifts at 3.0 t, 5 reach trucks at 2.0 t, 11 electric pallet jacks and 12 hand pallet jacks. No other forklifts, reach trucks or powered pallet trucks are held or hired without warehouse manager approval, and any temporary hire must be electric and at or above the same ratings where used in Zone B high bays.

7. The fleet is completed by fixed handling equipment. Each of the 8 dock doors at 1.2 m dock height has its own dock leveller operated only by trained staff. Dispatch operates 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers in Zone D for wrapping every outbound pallet to a stable load, and the site operates 1 cardboard baler for packing waste. These are electric powered and maintained by the maintenance technician.

8. Control and data equipment is part of the fleet. The teams share 20 handheld WMS scanners used for booking in Zone A, put-away to Zone B, E and F, replenishment to Zone C, scan verification in Zone C and packing and labelling in Zone D. Availability of scanners is planned per shift by the shift supervisor; no paper or verbal substitute is permitted for scanner tasks.

9. Allocation of equipment follows role and zone discipline under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. Only authorised forklift operators drive the 9 counterbalance forklifts and 5 reach trucks; other roles use only the electric and hand pallet jacks for which they are trained. No truck or jack may be taken outside its designated zones or used to exceed the 900 kg pallet limit, the 2,700 kg bay limit, or the 3-pallet and 4.0 m block-stack limit.

title: Authorisation and Daily Checks
text:
### ops.ch09.s2 Authorisation and Daily Checks

1. Authorisation and daily checks for all MHE are governed by PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. The principle is fixed: no licence, no truck. No person may drive any powered truck on site without first being authorised as a forklift operator, and no powered truck may be used on any shift without a documented pre-use check for that day.

2. Only the warehouse manager may authorise a new forklift operator. Authorisation requires a valid forklift licence for the equipment class, a documented practical assessment on Harborwick equipment and zones, and a dated record stating name, licence number and expiry, equipment types authorised — 3.0 t counterbalance forklift, 2.0 t reach truck and electric pallet jack — and the manager's signature. No shift supervisor, dispatcher or other role may grant, extend or renew driving authority.

3. Authorisation is equipment-specific and record-held. A licence alone does not confer authority to drive on site, and authority on one truck type does not transfer to another. The register of authorised operators is kept in the office annex and on the floor, and the shift supervisor must verify against it before tasking any operator to the 9 counterbalance forklifts, the 5 reach trucks or the 11 electric pallet jacks. Floaters and other roles may never drive counterbalance or reach trucks unless they hold a current licence and appear on this register as authorised.

4. Hand pallet jacks are not licence-controlled but are task-controlled. The 12 hand pallet jacks may be used only by staff trained and assigned to that task by the shift supervisor for Zone A, Zone C or Zone D low-level moves. Training is recorded, and no untrained person may use any MHE, powered or manual, in any zone.

5. Every powered truck — each of the 9 counterbalance forklifts, each of the 5 reach trucks and each of the 11 electric pallet jacks — must receive a documented pre-use check before its first use each day, on every shift on which it is used including Saturday overtime. The check is carried out by the assigned authorised operator using the PR-10 daily check sheet for that truck ID, and is signed with name, date, time and truck hours before the truck leaves its park position.

6. The daily check covers battery charge and condition, tyres and wheels, forks, backrest and chains, mast and reach mechanism, brakes, steering, lights, horn, reversing alarm, safety belt, emergency stop and hydraulic leaks, with load plate and capacity markings legible. For reach trucks the check includes bay-height interlocks where fitted; for counterbalance trucks it includes fork locking and tilt. Any defect, warning light, fluid leak, damaged fork or chain, faulty brake, steering or alarm is a fail.

7. A truck that fails its daily check is grounded immediately. The operator must not drive it, must tag it DO NOT USE, and must report it to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician at once. The supervisor removes the truck from service, reassigns work to a serviceable truck, and records the grounding in the PR-10 log and PR-15 handover. The maintenance technician inspects, repairs and logs the action with date, truck ID and work done; only the technician may clear a grounded truck back into service with a signed release.

8. Check sheets are retained as the audit trail for PR-10. A missing, incomplete or unsigned sheet means the truck has not been checked and must not be used. The shift supervisor verifies at shift start that every powered truck planned for use that shift has a completed daily check for that day, that no grounded truck is in use, and that only authorised operators are assigned to driving tasks.

9. Authorisation is withdrawn on licence expiry, on medical restriction, after any impact, tip or pedestrian near-miss, or on repeated procedural breach. Re-authorisation requires manager review and, where required, retraining and reassessment before the name is restored to the register. No person may self-certify fitness to drive, and no verbal clearance overrides a grounding or a lapsed authorisation.

title: Safe Operation
text:
### ops.ch09.s3 Safe Operation

1. Safe operation of all MHE is governed by PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation together with PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. This section applies to every authorised operator of the 9 counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t, the 5 reach trucks rated at 2.0 t, the 11 electric pallet jacks and the 12 hand pallet jacks, on every shift including authorised Saturday overtime.

2. Forklift operators must wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving, no exceptions. Seat belts are fitted to the counterbalance forklifts and reach trucks and must be fastened before the truck moves from its park position and remain fastened for the entire travel, lifting and manoeuvring cycle. No truck may be driven with a missing, damaged or bypassed belt, and the belt is checked as part of the documented daily check before first use each day.

3. Inside the building the maximum speed is 10 km/h. This limit applies from the dock threshold inward to all movement in Zones A to F, including the 4.0 m main transport aisles and the 3.0 m rack-storage aisles in Zone B and Zone C. Operators must travel slower than 10 km/h whenever load, aisle width, congestion, visibility or floor condition requires it, with forks or pallet low and load stable.

4. In the fenced yard of approximately 3,500 m2 the limit is 12 km/h for all carriers and any Harborwick MHE operating outside. Wherever people and trucks meet the limit is 5 km/h and this always overrides the others. The 5 km/h zone covers every marked pedestrian zone, every zebra crossing between the 1.2 m walkways and an aisle, and every dock ramp and leveller area at the eight doors at 1.2 m dock height.

5. The aisle network is fixed and determines safe operation. Main transport aisles feeding zones and docks are 4.0 m wide; rack-storage aisles between rack rows are 3.0 m wide; pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide and physically separated by continuous yellow barriers. No MHE may use a walkway, no pedestrian may walk in a transport or rack aisle, and no pallet, waste, film or idle truck may be staged in any 4.0 m or 3.0 m aisle or on a crossing.

6. At every marked crossing the MHE operator must give way to pedestrians, reduce to 5 km/h, sound the horn on approach to blind rack ends, corners and ramp entries, and be prepared to stop. Operators must not overtake or queue across a crossing, must not reverse on a ramp without observation, and must stop and seek banksman guidance if the load blocks forward view. Pedestrians must use only the 1.2 m barrier walkways.

7. Loads must remain within site limits at all times: no pallet over 900 kg, load included, no rack bay in Zone B over 2,700 kg total, and no block-stack outside racking over 3 pallets high and 4.0 m overall. Loads must be centred, stable and within the fork and bay envelope, with mast tilted back for travel and forks kept low. Two pallets must never be carried as a single load to avoid limits.

8. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor, and this applies equally during MHE operations. The shift supervisor on duty owns enforcement of seat-belt use, speed compliance and aisle and walkway discipline, and stops any unsafe travel, overloaded pallet or barrier breach immediately.

9. Any contact, tip, overload, near-miss or speed breach involving MHE stops that truck immediately. The operator reports to the shift supervisor, the truck is tagged DO NOT USE and grounded pending maintenance technician inspection, and the incident is logged under PR-10 and handed over under PR-15. Authorisation to drive is withdrawn pending review by the warehouse manager.

title: Returns Intake and Inspection
text:
1. Returns intake and inspection is governed by PR-07 Returns handling and takes place only in Zone F — services and control. Zone F covers 600 m2 and houses returns inspection, quarantine, value-added packing and the separate 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage. No returns may be received, held, inspected or staged in Zones A, B, C, D or E.

2. Only goods returned within 14 days of delivery are accepted. The 14-day count runs from the recorded delivery date to the return arrival date shown on the carrier paperwork and dispatcher schedule. Goods presented after 14 days, without proof of delivery date, or for a client or order not on the schedule are not accepted and remain with the carrier pending dispatcher and shift supervisor instruction.

3. All return vehicles are pre-booked by the dispatcher with a specific door assignment and time slot. Returns are scheduled as inbound movements at Doors 1-4 at 1.2 m dock height, each with its own leveller operated only by trained staff when the vehicle is positioned and braked. No returns movement may be scheduled or handled at outbound Doors 5-8, and no vehicle may be unloaded without dispatcher release.

4. On arrival at the assigned inbound door, paperwork is checked before unloading: delivery note, original order or delivery reference, carrier note, product and quantity being returned, reason for return, batch or lot and expiry where applicable, and any temperature or hazmat note. Returns are then moved directly to the designated returns inspection lanes in Zone F via the 4.0 m main transport aisles. They must not be counted as available stock in Zone A, placed in Zone B, E or D, or staged outside Zone F.

5. Only the 4 returns and packing staff, under the shift supervisor on duty, carry out returns inspection in Zone F. Inspection is by unit and is completed for every returned carton and unit before any disposition is proposed. Pallet-level checks, sampling or manager override of inspection are not permitted.

6. Every unit is inspected in Zone F against its paperwork, original label, batch or expiry and the stated return reason. Inspection covers packaging integrity, seal and tamper evidence, wet, crushed or opened cartons, label match, count versus paperwork, expiry or date-code, clean condition and, for chilled returns, surface temperature against the +2 °C to +8 °C range. Hazmat returns are inspected only in the 60 m2 ventilated cage area in Zone F under PR-13, subject to the 4,000 kg cage limit and compatibility plan, and are never unpacked outside the cage.

7. All inspections are recorded on the PR-07 returns record with carrier, door, date, client, SKU, quantity returned, quantity inspected, condition, batch or expiry, name and signature. The 20 handheld WMS scanners are used to log receipt of returns as held in Zone F, not as available stock. Shortages, overages, wrong product or undocumented items are logged as PR-07 exceptions and handed over under PR-15.

8. Any damaged, leaking, contaminated, seal-failed or temperature-excursion unit found during returns inspection is segregated immediately, labelled HOLD with reason, date and finder, and transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Such units remain in quarantine and are not available for restock, rework or dispatch until disposition is approved and recorded.

9. No returned goods may be returned to stock in Zone B, Zone C or Zone E, sent for rework, or scrapped until inspection of every unit is complete and the PR-07 proposal of restock, rework or scrap is recorded. Returns staff propose disposition only; final approval is by the shift supervisor. All returns remaining in Zone F at shift change are reported in the PR-15 handover as held, not available.

title: Disposition and Write-Offs
text:
1. Disposition of inspected returns and quarantine stock is governed by PR-07 Returns handling together with PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Both procedures operate only in Zone F — services and control — which houses quarantine, returns inspection and the separate 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage. No disposition decision is made outside Zone F and no quarantined or held goods may be moved to Zone B, Zone C, Zone E or Zone D until disposition is approved and recorded.

2. Every returned unit must have completed unit-level inspection in Zone F before any disposition is proposed. The 4 returns and packing staff record a disposition proposal for each inspected unit as one of three outcomes only: restock to available stock, rework via value-added packing in Zone F, or scrap and removal. Proposals are entered on the PR-07 record with SKU, batch or lot and expiry where applicable, quantity, condition, reason, value and name and signature. Sampling, pallet-level proposals or verbal recommendations are not valid.

3. Final approval of disposition of inspected returns rests solely with the shift supervisor on duty. Returns and packing staff may propose only; no unit may be restocked, sent for rework or scrapped until the supervisor has reviewed the PR-07 inspection, confirmed the quantity and condition, and signed the decision with name, role, date and time. The supervisor verifies that goods meet client restock criteria, that cold-chain goods inspected against +2 °C to +8 °C are within range, and that hazmat returns remain inside the 60 m2 cage in Zone F under PR-13 and within the 4,000 kg cage limit.

4. Damaged, leaking, contaminated, seal-failed or temperature-excursion goods found at any point — in Zone A receiving, Zone B bulk storage, Zone C picking, Zone D dispatch or Zone E cold zone — are transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found under PR-09. In quarantine they are labelled HOLD with reason, finder, date and value estimate, physically segregated from any other Zone F stock, and recorded as not available in the WMS. No damaged goods are retained in their originating zone.

5. Goods in quarantine remain in quarantine until the applicable write-off or disposition approval is documented. For damaged-goods write-offs, approval is by value threshold: the shift supervisor may approve a write-off up to and including 750 EUR per incident; any write-off above 750 EUR, individually or when aggregated for the same incident, requires written approval by the warehouse manager. Goods must not be destroyed, returned to stock or released to a carrier pending the required signature.

6. The warehouse manager retains sole authority for write-offs above 750 EUR and for sign-off of the annual wall-to-wall stocktake from which stocktake adjustments arise. The manager reviews the PR-09 quarantine tag, incident report, count sheets and recount where applicable, and value calculation before signing. The threshold is inclusive of the supervisor's limit, and splitting a single damage event into smaller amounts to avoid manager approval is prohibited.

7. Execution follows the approved disposition. Restock is booked into the WMS via one of the 20 handheld scanners, labelled and put away only to a valid location in Zone B within the 2,700 kg bay limit and 900 kg pallet limit, or to Zone E where chilled, or to Zone C pick faces via PR-03 replenishment. Rework is carried out in Zone F value-added packing and re-inspected before booking. Scrap is segregated, defaced where required, and removed under the supervisor's control with quantity and method recorded.

8. All quarantine movements, approvals andwrite-offs are recorded as the audit trail: PR-07 inspection and proposal, PR-09 HOLD tag and quarantine location, supervisor or manager approval with name, role, date and signature, WMS booking or scrap removal reference, and handover entry under PR-15. Any write-off, whether approved by supervisor or manager, is posted only after the record is complete and the goods have left quarantine in the system.

9. At each PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover the outgoing supervisor hands over all open PR-07 and PR-09 cases: pallets and units held in quarantine in Zone F, hazmat cage quantity against the 4,000 kg limit, proposals awaiting supervisor decision, write-offs awaiting manager approval, and any damaged goods transferred that shift. The incoming supervisor verifies that no quarantined or held stock is shown as available and that no disposition has been executed without the required approval.

title: Cycle Counting
text:
### ops.ch11.s1 Cycle Counting

1. Cycle counting is governed by PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts and runs every working day, Monday to Friday, on a rotating zone schedule. PR-08 provides the daily check that the stock in the system is the stock on the rack and is separate from the annual wall-to-wall stocktake. No zone containing booked stock is excluded from the rotation.

2. Ownership of cycle counting rests with the 2 stock controllers. They own inventory accuracy day to day: they plan the rotating schedule, execute the counts, conduct second counts and recounts, and prepare adjustments for approval. No other role may close a PR-08 count or post an adjustment.

3. The rotating schedule covers all zones holding booked stock: Zone B bulk storage with 2,400 pallet positions, Zone C picking faces and flow racks, Zone D staged outbound pallets where held overnight, Zone E cold zone and Zone F quarantine and the 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage. Zones are counted in turn so that every location is counted at least once within the rotation cycle, with frequency weighted to high-movement SKUs in Zone C and high-value locations.

4. Counts are carried out using the 20 handheld WMS scanners against live WMS tasks. Each task specifies zone, aisle, bay, level and position, SKU, batch or lot and expiry where applicable, and expected quantity. Counting is blind where the WMS is configured blind, and the stock controller scans location label first, then counts physical stock by handling unit and carton, then enters the count.

5. Counting takes place within the normal shift window of 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, planned by the shift supervisor to avoid conflict with replenishment to Zone C, put-away to Zone B and loading at Doors 5-8. In Zone E doors are kept closed except for access and counts are completed quickly to maintain +2 °C to +8 °C. In Zone F quarantine and hazmat locations are counted as held stock, not as available, with the hazmat cage checked against the 4,000 kg limit.

6. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Where first count does not match the system, the WMS blocks adjustment and generates a second-count task. The second count is carried out by a second stock controller or, where only one is on shift, by the shift supervisor acting as second counter; a person may not second-count their own first count. Only when the second count is entered does PR-08 permit an adjustment proposal.

7. Discrepancies are recorded as PR-08 exceptions with location, SKU, batch, quantity expected, quantity found, variance, name, date and time. Damaged, leaking or seal-failed goods found during counting are not counted as available, are labelled HOLD, and are transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09. Any evidence of rack damage, overload above 2,700 kg per bay, or pallet over 900 kg found during the count is reported to the shift supervisor and maintenance technician immediately.

8. Adjustments arising from the second count are prepared by the stock controllers with root cause — mis-scan, put-away error, replenishment short, picking variance — and are posted in the WMS only after verification. The WMS retains the full audit trail of first count, second count, adjustment, name and time. Goods remaining unbooked in Zone A are not counted as available stock and must not be adjusted into availability.

9. Completion of the day's PR-08 cycle counts, outstanding second counts, adjustments proposed and posted, and any zones carried over is recorded in the PR-08 log and handed over at PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover. The outgoing shift supervisor verifies that aisles used for counting are clear, that 4.0 m transport aisles, 3.0 m rack aisles and 1.2 m walkways remain unobstructed, and that no location is left with an unresolved variance without a named owner for the next shift.

title: Annual Wall-to-Wall Stocktake
text:
1. The annual wall-to-wall stocktake is governed by PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts as the full physical verification of all booked stock on site. It is a single scheduled event each year, separate from the daily rotating cycle counts, and requires a complete operational shutdown of the hall. Its purpose is to verify that the quantity in the WMS matches the quantity on the rack in every storage location.

2. The warehouse manager is accountable for the annual stocktake and is the only approver for its result. The manager authorises the stocktake date, approves the shutdown plan and overtime needed, and provides the final sign-off that closes the stocktake. No stocktake is closed and no system-wide adjustment from it is posted without the manager's dated signature.

3. The stocktake is carried out with the site shut down for warehousing operations. On the stocktake day there is no inbound receiving at Doors 1-4, no put-away to Zone B, Zone E or Zone F, no PR-03 replenishment to Zone C, no PR-04 picking in Zone C and no outbound staging or loading in Zone D at Doors 5-8. The dispatcher clears all carrier slots for the shutdown window and the yard is held clear except for the stocktake.

4. Preparation is owned by the manager with the 2 stock controllers and the shift supervisors. The WMS is frozen at a recorded cut-off time, all open PR-01 receipts in Zone A are segregated as unbooked and not counted as available, Zone D is cleared of staged loads or held over as counted staged stock, and Zones B, C, E and F are tidied with every pallet in a labelled location within the 900 kg pallet limit, 2,700 kg bay limit and 4,000 kg hazmat cage limit in the 60 m2 ventilated cage in Zone F.

5. Counting is executed by teams led by the 2 stock controllers under the shift supervisor on duty, using the 20 handheld WMS scanners. Every location holding booked stock is counted location by location: Zone B with 2,400 pallet positions including block-stack and high-bay racking, Zone C pick faces and flow racks, Zone D any staged pallets, Zone E cold zone held between +2 °C and +8 °C with doors kept closed, and Zone F services and control including quarantine as held, not available, and the hazmat cage checked against the 4,000 kg limit.

6. Each count task specifies zone, aisle, bay, level and position, SKU, batch or lot and expiry where applicable. The counter scans the location label first, counts physical handling units and cartons by hand, then enters the count on the scanner. Counts are blind where configured, and no estimate, paperwork quantity or memory count is permitted. Damaged or leaking goods found during the count are labelled HOLD and transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09 and are not counted as available.

7. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Where a first count does not match the system quantity, the WMS blocks adjustment and generates a second-count task. The second count is carried out by a second stock controller or by the shift supervisor acting as second counter; a person may not second-count their own first count. The variance is recorded with location, SKU, batch, quantity expected, quantity found, name, date and time.

8. On completion of first and second counts, the stock controllers reconcile the WMS freeze against the counted quantities and prepare the variance report by client, SKU and zone with root cause where known — mis-scan, put-away error, replenishment short or picking variance. All count sheets, recount sheets, scanner histories and quarantine tags are collated for the manager's review.

9. The manager reviews the full pack — count sheets, second counts, variance report, and any damaged-goods write-offs arising, noting that write-offs above 750 EUR per incident require the manager's own approval. Only when satisfied, the manager applies a dated signature to close the stocktake in the PR-08 log, and only then are system-wide adjustments posted in the WMS. The signed pack forms the audit trail and is handed over under PR-15 before normal operations in Zones A to F and at the eight dock doors resume.

title: Adjustments and Recounts
text:
1. Adjustments and recounts are governed by PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. The rule is absolute: no adjustment is ever posted without a second count. This applies to every variance found during daily cycle counts and during the annual wall-to-wall stocktake, in every zone holding booked stock.

2. An adjustment means any change to the WMS quantity, whether arising from a cycle count variance, a recount discrepancy or a stocktake variance. This includes increases and decreases, batch or lot corrections and corrections to Zone B, Zone C, Zone E and Zone F including quarantine and the 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage. Goods segregated as unbooked in Zone A are never adjusted into availability.

3. The WMS enforces the control. Where a first count does not match the system expected quantity, the WMS blocks any adjustment for that location and generates a second-count task. The location remains locked for adjustment until the second count is entered, and no manual override, paper adjustment or verbal instruction may bypass the block.

4. The first count is carried out by a stock controller using one of the 20 handheld WMS scanners. The task specifies zone, aisle, bay, level and position, SKU, batch or lot and expiry where applicable, and expected quantity. The counter scans the location label first, counts physical handling units and cartons by hand, then enters the count. Estimating or using paperwork quantity is not permitted.

5. The second count is independent. It is carried out by the second stock controller or, where only one is on shift, by the shift supervisor acting as second counter. A person may not second-count their own first count. The second counter repeats the same scan-location, count-physical, enter-quantity sequence blind to the first result, with name, date and time recorded.

6. Where the second count matches the system, the first count is recorded as error and no adjustment is posted; the cause — mis-scan, mis-count or obstructed label — is logged as a PR-08 exception. Where the second count confirms the first count and a variance remains, the variance is proven and an adjustment proposal is prepared with location, SKU, batch, quantity expected, quantity found, variance, value and root cause.

7. Ownership of adjustment proposals rests with the 2 stock controllers. They prepare the proposal, attach first-count and second-count records and scanner history, and present it for verification. Damaged, leaking or seal-failed goods found during either count are not counted as available, are labelled HOLD and transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09, and any write-off follows the approval threshold.

8. Posting is controlled by verification. Cycle-count adjustments are posted in the WMS only after the second count is entered and the proposal verified; stocktake adjustments are posted only after the full stocktake pack is reviewed and signed off by the warehouse manager, who alone signs off the annual wall-to-wall result. Write-offs above 750 EUR per incident aggregated require the manager's written approval; the shift supervisor may approve only up to and including 750 EUR.

9. Every count, second count and adjustment is retained as the audit trail in the PR-08 log: first count, second count, adjustment, name, role and time, with variance report for the stocktake. Outstanding second counts and pending adjustments are handed over at PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover, and no location is left with an unresolved variance without a named owner for the next shift.

title: Racking and Equipment Maintenance
text:
### ops.ch12.s1 Racking and Equipment Maintenance

1. Racking and equipment maintenance is owned by the 1 maintenance technician and covers all racking, MHE and fixed dock equipment on site. The technician carries out planned checks, responds to faults reported by the shift supervisor, and logs every repair with date, equipment and action taken. No racking, truck or dock equipment is returned to service until the technician has cleared it with a signed release.

2. High-bay pallet racking in Zone B with 2,400 pallet positions is subject to a documented safety inspection every month. The inspection is carried out by the maintenance technician with the shift supervisor on duty, using the racking inspection sheet by aisle, bay, level and position. Completion is recorded with date, names and signatures in the racking log and handed over under PR-15.

3. The monthly check verifies uprights, feet, bracing and beams for impact, deformation or missing lock pins, beam deflection, correct beam levels within the 10 m clear height, legible bay rating plates at 2,700 kg per bay, and that no bay is loaded beyond 2,700 kg total and no pallet exceeds the site limit of 900 kg. Free block-stacking areas are checked for the 3-pallet and 4.0 m limit, vertical stability and marked floor locations clear of the 4.0 m main and 3.0 m rack-storage aisles.

4. Any bay found damaged, overloaded, impacted or showing bay-caution load is taken out of service immediately. The shift supervisor ensures the bay is emptied where safe to do so, physically blocked with barrier and tag DO NOT USE, and recorded as out of service with bay ID, reason, finder and time. Put-away to that bay via the 2.0 t reach trucks or 3.0 t counterbalance forklifts is prohibited until cleared.

5. Every repair to racking is entered in the repair log with date, location, defect, cause where known, corrective action, parts replaced and name and signature. Impact damage, overload correction and beam replacement are notified to the warehouse manager where the incident report threshold is met. The bay is only cleared back into service after re-inspection by the maintenance technician and removal of the block and tag.

6. The powered fleet — 9 counterbalance forklifts at 3.0 t, 5 reach trucks at 2.0 t, 11 electric pallet jacks and 12 hand pallet jacks — is maintained in a planned programme separate from the PR-10 documented daily check before first use each day. The technician carries out scheduled servicing by truck ID and hours, tyre, fork, chain, mast, brake, steering, lights, horn, battery and charger checks, and responds to any truck grounded with a fail, tagged DO NOT USE.

7. Fixed equipment is inspected monthly alongside racking: 8 dock levellers at 1.2 m dock height at Doors 1-4 inbound and Doors 5-8 outbound for seating, lip, controls and safety stops, 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers in Zone D and 1 cardboard baler for guards, interlocks and electrics, and the 20 handheld WMS scanners and charging stations for availability. Leveller faults are reported to the shift supervisor and the door taken out of service until cleared.

8. Cold Zone E and the 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F equipment is included in the technician's rounds where it relates to racking, doors, seals, ventilation and spill equipment, with temperature alarms and refrigeration faults escalated immediately. No repair is carried out on live cold or hazmat locations without the shift supervisor securing the area and segregating stock as held where required.

9. All racking inspections, MHE servicing and fixed-equipment repairs are retained as the audit trail: monthly inspection sheets, grounding tags, release signatures and the repair log with date, equipment and action. Outstanding rack bays out of service, trucks grounded and doors out of service are handed over at each PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover with named owner until closed.

title: Cold-Chain and Hazmat Response
text:
### ops.ch12.s2 Cold-Chain and Hazmat Response

1. Cold-chain handling in Zone E is governed by PR-12 Cold-chain handling and hazmat control in Zone F is governed by PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. Zone E covers 300 m2 and is held continuously between +2 °C and +8 °C; the separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2 in Zone F holds all hazardous materials on site subject to the 4,000 kg cage limit. Both procedures run on every shift including authorised Saturday overtime.

2. Zone E is monitored by continuous automatic temperature alarms with audible and visual alert on the floor and in the office annex, backed by manual verification each shift. The shift supervisor ensures a trained operator records the displayed Zone E temperature at least once per shift — morning 06:00-14:00 and afternoon 14:00-22:00 — with zone, reading, date, time, name and signature in the PR-12 log. Door seals, closures and air-circulation units are checked as part of that verification.

3. Any alarm or manual reading outside +2 °C to +8 °C is treated as an immediate excursion. The shift supervisor stops all put-away to and issue from Zone E, secures the cold-zone doors closed, segregates affected stock in place as held and labelled HOLD, and notifies the warehouse manager and maintenance technician at once. No held chilled stock may be released to replenishment for Zone C, to staging in Zone D or back to bulk storage until the cause is rectified.

4. Stock affected by an excursion remains held until temperature is restored, stabilised within +2 °C to +8 °C and documented, and disposition is recorded under PR-12. The supervisor verifies the alarm log, the manual verification entries and the duration of exposure before approving return to available stock, transfer to quarantine in Zone F under PR-09, or scrap. Any damaged, leaking or seal-failed chilled goods found are transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day and are not retained in Zone E.

5. The hazmat cage of 60 m2 in Zone F is kept locked, ventilated, clearly signed and within the 4,000 kg limit at all times, with incompatible classes segregated by the PR-13 compatibility plan. Ventilation, cage integrity, segregation markings and the live cage inventory by weight and pallet count are checked each shift by the shift supervisor. At the pallet limit of 900 kg this is at most 4 full-weight pallets in the cage, and no receipt that would exceed 4,000 kg may be released to put-away.

6. PR-13 spill readiness is fixed at the cage. Suitable spill kits, absorbents, neutralisers where applicable and PPE are stationed at the cage entrance outside the locked area, with clear instructions by hazmat class. No hazmat may be staged, queued or held outside the ventilated cage in Zone F, even temporarily in Zone A or Zone D, except for the sealed load on the vehicle at the door before inspection, and hazmat arriving without correct documentation or with damaged packaging is not unloaded beyond the door.

7. Any leak, spill, damaged container, vapour or alarm in the cage in Zone F is an immediate incident under PR-13. The finder cordons the area, secures ignition sources where relevant, dons required PPE, contains the spill only if safe to do so, and notifies the shift supervisor at once. The supervisor stops all movement to and from Zone F, evacuates the immediate area where required, calls the maintenance technician, and escalates to the warehouse manager and emergency services where thresholds are met.

8. The maintenance technician owns all alarm, refrigeration, ventilation and containment equipment for PR-12 and PR-13. The technician responds to every temperature alarm, sensor fault, refrigeration failure, door-seal defect, ventilation failure or spill-equipment defect, secures the area with the shift supervisor, carries out repair and logs every action with date, equipment, location, fault and corrective work. No alarm is silenced without investigation and no cold or hazmat location is returned to service until the technician has cleared it with a signed release.

9. All PR-12 and PR-13 events form the audit trail and are handed over under PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover: alarm activations, manual verification readings, excursions and holds, hazmat cage quantity against the 4,000 kg limit, ventilation and spill-kit status, quarantined goods under PR-09 and open incidents. The outgoing supervisor records the state with names and times and the incoming supervisor verifies alarms armed, doors sealed, cage locked and within limit, and kits complete before operations restart.

title: Evacuation and Assembly
text:
1. Evacuation and assembly is governed by PR-14 Emergency evacuation. It applies to every person on site — Harborwick staff, office annex staff, drivers in the yard and any visitor — on all shifts including authorised Saturday overtime. The assembly point is fixed at the marked roll-call area by the north fence.

2. Any activation of the fire alarm, evacuation siren or verbal evacuation order from the shift supervisor is a full evacuation. All work stops immediately: PR-01 receiving at Doors 1-4, put-away to Zone B, E and F, PR-03 replenishment, PR-04 picking in Zone C, wrapping and staging in Zone D at Doors 5-8, and all MHE movement. Operators park trucks safely where standing, lower forks, apply brakes and leave keys where procedure requires.

3. Evacuation is by the nearest designated personnel exit via the 1.2 m yellow-barrier walkways and marked escape routes. Dock doors and levellers at 1.2 m dock height are not escape routes unless signed as such. The 4.0 m main transport aisles and 3.0 m rack-storage aisles are evacuation routes and must never be blocked; running, use of lifts, or re-entry to collect belongings is prohibited.

4. The shift supervisor on duty owns the evacuation and assembly. The supervisor triggers the alarm where needed, ensures the hall, office annex, Zone E cold zone, Zone F including the 60 m2 ventilated hazmat cage, and dock areas are cleared, and directs all persons to the assembly point by the north fence using the walkways and yard one-way system. The warehouse manager is notified as soon as practicable.

5. At the assembly point the shift supervisor conducts roll call against the live attendance for that shift: clocked staff, floaters, dispatchers, maintenance technician, office annex presence and the driver waiting-area log. Drivers called forward from the fenced yard of approximately 3,500 m2 and any carrier waiting at the gate are included. No person is marked present by assumption.

6. No person may re-enter the building, the hall, the office annex link or the yard dock ramp area until the roll call is complete and all persons are accounted for. Re-entry is authorised only by the shift supervisor after confirmation from the fire service or designated responsible person that the site is safe, following headcount at the north fence. No supervisor may authorise re-entry on incomplete count.

7. An evacuation drill is carried out every quarter under PR-14. The drill is scheduled by the warehouse manager with the shift supervisors and dispatchers, covers both the 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00 shift patterns in rotation, and tests alarm, evacuation by zones A to F, assembly and roll call at the north fence. The date, time, zones involved, alarm type and attendance are recorded with names and signatures.

8. After any real evacuation or drill the shift supervisor records the PR-14 log: trigger, evacuation time, assembly time, roll-call result, any missing persons or delays, barriers or crossings used, and any defect to exits, signage, lighting or barriers. Faults are reported to the maintenance technician immediately and the exit or route taken out of use until cleared.

9. Outstanding PR-14 actions — incomplete drill, open defect to exits, barriers, assembly signage or north-fence roll-call equipment — are handed over under PR-15 End-of-Shift Handover. The outgoing supervisor records the state and the incoming supervisor verifies that escape routes, 1.2 m walkways, yard approaches and the north-fence assembly point are clear and marked before operations restart.

chapter_title: Chapter 1 - Traffic Management: Forklifts and Pedestrians
title: 1.1 Speed Limits and Transport Routes
text:
## hs.ch01.s1 1.1 Speed Limits and Transport Routes

1. Harborwick 3PL operates a single enforced speed regime across the entire site. The limits apply to all electric forklifts, reach trucks and electric pallet jacks, as well as to any contractor or visitor vehicle permitted in the yard. Exceeding a limit is treated as unsafe driving and will be stopped immediately.

2. Inside the warehouse hall the maximum speed is 8 km/h. This limit applies everywhere inside the building, including Zones A to F, and covers all internal transport aisles and storage aisles.

3. In the fenced yard outside the hall the maximum speed is 15 km/h. The yard area of approximately 3,500 m2 is used for vehicle manoeuvring and access to the eight dock doors. The 15 km/h limit applies to the full yard unless a lower limit is posted.

4. Wherever pedestrians and trucks meet the maximum speed is 5 km/h. This reduced limit is mandatory and overrides the general limits above. It applies at all times in the following locations:
   a) marked pedestrian zones;
   b) marked pedestrian crossings;
   c) the dock ramps and the immediate approach to dock doors 1-8.

5. Drivers must slow to 5 km/h in good time before entering a shared zone and must be prepared to stop for pedestrians. Pedestrians have priority at all crossings and in all marked pedestrian zones.

6. Speed limits are posted at the hall entrances, at the yard entrance and at each transition to a 5 km/h zone. Drivers must observe signage and floor markings. Lack of signage does not exempt drivers from the limits stated in this instruction.

7. Main transport aisles inside the hall are 4.0 m wide. These aisles provide the primary routes for forklift and pallet truck movement between zones and to the dock doors. Drivers must keep to the main transport aisles for longer moves and must not cut through picking or staging areas except to access a designated bay.

8. Rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide. This width applies to all aisles within high-bay pallet racking in Zone B and to other racked storage aisles. Drivers operating counterbalance forklifts and reach trucks must account for load width and turning clearance and must not enter a rack aisle if the load or vehicle exceeds safe clearance.

9. Pedestrian walkways are physically separated from vehicle routes by fixed yellow barriers. Walkways are 1.2 m wide and are marked on the floor. Vehicles must never enter, park on or block a pedestrian walkway. Pedestrians must use the walkways and designated crossings when moving through the warehouse and yard.

10. Speed and route discipline is monitored by the shift supervisor in charge of the floor. Any speeding, failure to slow at crossings and ramps, or misuse of pedestrian walkways and transport aisles must be reported immediately and is subject to action under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation and PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse.

chapter_title: Chapter 1 - Traffic Management: Forklifts and Pedestrians
title: 1.2 Segregated Pedestrian Walkways and Dock Discipline
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL operates on strict segregation of people and trucks. Pedestrians and mobile equipment use physically separate routes at all times. Any presence of a person on foot in a vehicle route, and any vehicle incursion onto a pedestrian route, is treated as an unsafe condition and must be stopped immediately in accordance with PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse and PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.

2. Pedestrian walkways are provided throughout the hall and in the yard approaches. They are 1.2 m wide, clearly marked on the floor and physically separated from vehicle routes by fixed yellow barriers. Walkways provide continuous protected access between the office annex, welfare facilities, all six zones (A-F), emergency exits and the assembly point.

3. Yellow barriers must remain in place and intact. They must not be moved, removed, driven through or used as a resting point for goods. Any damage, displacement or obstruction of a barrier or floor marking must be reported immediately to the shift supervisor and to the maintenance technician for repair.

4. No vehicle may enter, park, stage loads or extend any part of a load over a pedestrian walkway. Drivers must keep within the 4.0 m main transport aisles for longer moves and the 3.0 m rack storage aisles for put-away and retrieval, and must never use a walkway to shortcut or turn.

5. Every person moving on foot inside the fence, including employees, visitors, contractors and drivers when outside their cab, must use the designated pedestrian walkways and designated crossings. Walking along or across transport aisles or dock ramps outside a crossing is prohibited except where a specific work task requires access to a bay, and then only after confirming the area is clear of moving trucks.

6. Pedestrian crossings are installed where walkways intersect transport aisles and at the approaches to the dock ramp area. At crossings the following discipline applies:
   a) pedestrians must stop at the barrier gate, look both ways and establish eye contact with any approaching driver before stepping out;
   b) drivers must already have slowed to the mandatory 5 km/h limit in advance of the crossing, be prepared to stop and give way to pedestrians;
   c) no overtaking, load stacking or parking is permitted at or immediately before a crossing.

7. The dock ramp area is a shared-risk zone. The 5 km/h limit applies on all ramps and on the immediate approach to dock doors 1-8. Pedestrians must not walk behind reversing vehicles, enter the ramp zone while levellers are in motion, or cross between a trailer and the dock edge.

8. Dock discipline is absolute. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and serve Zone A receiving; doors 5-8 are outbound only and serve Zone D dispatch. All doors are at 1.2 m dock height and are fitted with individual levellers, which may only be operated by authorised warehouse staff.

9. No carrier may arrive, wait at or occupy a dock door without dispatcher assignment. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling and assigns every carrier a specific door and time slot in accordance with PR-01 Inbound receiving and PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Drivers must follow the assigned slot and door; swapping doors without dispatcher approval is prohibited.

10. Drivers must report on arrival and then wait in the marked driver waiting area in the yard. Drivers are not permitted inside the warehouse hall at any time, except when explicitly escorted for a safety reason. Communication with drivers is conducted by the dispatcher or shift supervisor at the waiting area or door office, not on the warehouse floor.

11. No unloading or loading may begin until authorised: in Zone A only after paperwork has been checked, and in Zone D only after the dispatcher has released the outbound load. Pedestrians must keep clear of a door during trailer manoeuvring, leveller deployment and forklift entry and exit.

12. The shift supervisor in charge of the floor monitors walkway use and dock discipline continuously. Any barrier breach, misuse of crossings, speeding on ramps, unauthorised door use or driver entry to the hall must be reported immediately, recorded and actioned under PR-10, PR-11 and the incident reporting process.

chapter_title: Chapter 1 - Traffic Management: Forklifts and Pedestrians
title: 1.3 Forklift Authorisation and Daily Checks
text:
## hs.ch01.s3 1.3 Forklift Authorisation and Daily Checks

1. Only authorised operators may drive powered mobile handling equipment at Harborwick 3PL. This rule covers all 9 counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t, all 5 reach trucks rated at 2.0 t for high-bay work, and all 11 electric pallet jacks. Hand pallet jacks may only be used by staff trained in their safe use. No person may operate any truck without valid authorisation.

2. Authorisation is granted personally by the Warehouse Manager. No licence, no truck. A valid external forklift licence, successful completion of site induction and practical assessment on the actual truck type to be used, and a written authorisation entry are all required before any driving is permitted.

3. Authorisation is specific to truck type. An operator authorised only for counterbalance forklifts is not authorised for reach trucks. Reach trucks may only be used in their intended areas, primarily the high-bay racking in Zone B, by operators specifically authorised for that type.

4. The list of authorised operators is maintained by the Warehouse Manager and displayed for reference by the shift supervisor. The shift supervisor must verify authorisation before assigning any driving task. Unauthorised use, lending of a truck to another person, or use of an unauthorised truck type is prohibited and will be stopped immediately under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.

5. Authorisation is withdrawn or suspended after any incident, near-miss, unsafe driving observation, or licence expiry, pending retraining and re-authorisation by the Warehouse Manager.

6. Every powered truck must receive a documented pre-use check before its first use on each working day. This applies to each forklift, reach truck and electric pallet jack. The check must be carried out by the assigned operator at the start of the shift and recorded on the daily check sheet for that truck, regardless of whether the truck was used on the previous shift.

7. The daily check must cover at minimum: brakes including parking brake, steering, controls, horn, lights and reversing alarm where fitted, seat belt condition and operation, forks and carriage, chains, tyres and wheels, hydraulic leaks, battery charge and connector condition, and emergency stop function. Any defect affecting safety makes the truck unserviceable.

8. If a defect is found the operator must not use the truck, must attach a DO NOT USE tag, remove the key where applicable, report immediately to the shift supervisor in charge of the floor, and notify the maintenance technician. The defect and tag-out must be logged and the truck must remain out of service until the maintenance technician has repaired and cleared it in writing.

9. Completed daily check sheets are handed to the shift supervisor at the start of the shift and filed for audit. A missing or unsigned sheet means the truck has not been cleared for use. The maintenance technician reviews the logs, carries out scheduled maintenance for trucks, racking and dock equipment, and records every repair.

10. Additional rules apply whenever a truck is moving: the driver must wear a seat belt, keep within the applicable speed limits of 8 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps, and use only the 4.0 m main transport aisles and 3.0 m rack aisles. Handheld WMS scanners, stretch wrappers, the cardboard baler and dock levellers are not to be used as driving aids and levellers may only be operated by authorised warehouse staff.

chapter_title: Chapter 2 - Personal Protection and Safety Accountability
title: 2.1 Mandatory PPE on the Warehouse Floor
text:
## hs.ch02.s1 2.1 Mandatory PPE on the Warehouse Floor

1. Mandatory personal protective equipment applies to the entire warehouse hall floor of 6,000 m2, covering all six zones A to F — receiving, bulk storage, picking, dispatch, cold zone and services and control — including all transport aisles, rack aisles, pedestrian walkways and dock ramp areas. There are no exceptions on the floor itself.

2. Every person on the warehouse floor must wear a high-visibility vest at all times. This applies to all employees, shift supervisors, the Warehouse Manager, visitors, contractors and drivers whenever they are permitted on the floor. The vest must be worn outermost, fastened and clearly visible from all sides, and must not be covered by coats, bags or other clothing.

3. Every person on the warehouse floor must wear class S3 safety footwear at all times. This applies equally to office staff entering the floor, to visitors and to contractors. Footwear must be fully laced and in serviceable condition. Trainers, low shoes, open shoes, sandals and any non-safety footwear are prohibited on the floor without exception.

4. High-visibility vests and S3 footwear must be in clean, undamaged condition and of correct size. Damaged, heavily soiled, split or worn footwear, or faded or torn vests that reduce visibility or protection, must be taken out of use and replaced immediately. Employees must not modify PPE or wear it in a way that reduces its function.

5. The Warehouse Manager is accountable for ensuring sufficient stocks of approved high-visibility vests and S3 footwear in appropriate sizes are available. The shift supervisor in charge of the floor checks compliance at the start of each shift and during patrols, and must stop anyone without correct PPE from entering or remaining on the floor.

6. No exemption exists for short visits, quick checks or escorted entry. Anyone who cannot be provided with correct high-visibility vest and S3 footwear must not enter the floor and must wait in the office annex or in the marked driver waiting area in the yard. Drivers, in accordance with dock discipline, are not permitted inside the hall at any time except when explicitly escorted for a safety reason, and then only with full mandatory PPE.

7. The mandatory PPE boundary is the entrance from the office annex to the hall and any pedestrian door to the yard. PPE must be put on before stepping onto the floor and must remain on until the person has left the floor. PPE must not be removed while inside Zones A to F, including while standing in walkways, at crossings or at dock doors.

8. Forklift-related protection is included in floor discipline. All operators of the 9 counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t, the 5 reach trucks rated at 2.0 t and the 11 electric pallet jacks must wear a seat belt whenever the truck is moving, in addition to wearing a high-visibility vest and S3 footwear. The seat belt is part of mandatory protection when driving and is checked as part of the documented daily pre-use check.

9. Task-specific additional PPE is required in addition to, never instead of, the mandatory vest and S3 footwear. Cold-zone work in Zone E and hazmat handling in the ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F require further protection as defined in PR-12 Cold-chain handling and PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. Standard high-visibility vest and S3 footwear remain mandatory underneath any additional item.

10. Failure to wear mandatory PPE is treated as an unsafe act. The shift supervisor must immediately instruct the person to leave the floor, record the observation, and report it for review. Repeated or deliberate non-compliance is actioned under PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse and PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.

chapter_title: Chapter 2 - Personal Protection and Safety Accountability
title: 2.2 Roles and Supervision for Safety
text:
## hs.ch02.s2 2.2 Roles and Supervision for Safety

1. Safety accountability at Harborwick 3PL is personal and fixed. The Warehouse Manager is accountable for the whole site — operations, safety and final sign-offs. This accountability cannot be delegated. The Warehouse Manager sets safe systems of work under PR-01 to PR-15, authorises operators and critical operations, and ensures that supervision, equipment, PPE and training are in place for both shifts, Monday to Friday 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, and any authorised Saturday overtime.

2. Each shift is run by one shift supervisor who is in charge of the floor for that shift. The shift supervisor directs all floor staff, monitors compliance with speed limits, walkway and dock discipline, and PPE, and is the first point of contact for any unsafe condition. In peak season the same supervision rule applies: no work starts without a designated shift supervisor present.

3. The shift supervisor is responsible for immediate incident response. On any injury, near-miss, spill, vehicle contact, rack strike or alarm, the shift supervisor stops the work, secures the area, provides first response, records the facts and reviews every incident report before it is closed. No person may re-enter an affected area or re-start work until the shift supervisor has cleared it.

4. Only the Warehouse Manager may authorise a new forklift operator. No licence, no truck. Authorisation requires a valid external licence, site induction and practical assessment on the specific type — 9 counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t, 5 reach trucks rated at 2.0 t, or 11 electric pallet jacks — and a written entry on the authorised operator list. The shift supervisor must verify this authorisation before assigning any driving task and must suspend driving after any incident pending re-authorisation.

5. Only the Warehouse Manager approves overtime. Saturday morning working in peak season and any extension beyond the rostered shift may only proceed with prior written approval from the Warehouse Manager.

6. Financial and inventory sign-offs are fixed by value and role. The Warehouse Manager signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results and any damaged-goods write-off above 750 EUR. The shift supervisor may approve damaged-goods write-offs up to 750 EUR. No stock adjustment may be posted without a second count, and stock controllers may only propose adjustments after cycle counts and recounts under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts.

7. Final disposition of inspected returns is approved by the shift supervisor. Returns staff in Zone F inspect every unit returned within 14 days of delivery and propose restock, rework or scrap under PR-07 Returns handling; goods move from quarantine only after the shift supervisor’s approval. Damaged goods found anywhere on site must be moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling.

8. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling. Only the dispatcher may assign carriers a specific door and time slot — doors 1-4 inbound only, doors 5-8 outbound only — and release an outbound load in Zone D for loading. Swapping doors or starting loading or unloading without dispatcher release is prohibited.

9. The maintenance technician is responsible for maintaining trucks, racking and dock equipment and for logging every repair. The technician clears a tagged-out truck back into service in writing after a defect, supports the monthly documented racking inspection, and rectifies reported damage to yellow barriers, floor markings, levellers and racking without delay.

10. All employees, including inbound operators, pickers, stock controllers, returns and packing staff, dispatchers and floaters, are responsible for working to this Instruction, wearing mandatory PPE, reporting hazards, and handing over safety issues at end of shift under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Accountability for site safety rests with the Warehouse Manager; supervision of safety on the floor rests with the shift supervisor in charge.

chapter_title: Chapter 3 - Restricted Zones: Cold, Hazmat and Safe Storage
title: 3.1 Cold Zone Work (Zone E)
text:
### hs.ch03.s1 3.1 Cold Zone Work (Zone E)

1. Zone E is the dedicated cold zone of 300 m2 within the 6,000 m2 hall. It provides chilled storage held between +2 °C and +6 °C inclusive for food and other temperature-sensitive packed consumer goods. No other zone provides chilled storage, and ambient goods must not be stored in Zone E.

2. The temperature in Zone E must remain within +2 °C to +6 °C at all times, including during put-away, replenishment, picking and stock counts. Goods are only put away to Zone E after inspection and booking in Zone A under PR-02 Put-away to storage, and all movements in Zone E are directed by WMS tasks.

3. Zone E is fitted with continuous temperature monitoring and audible and visual alarms that activate immediately if the temperature falls below +2 °C or rises above +6 °C. On any alarm the person present must leave the zone safely, close the door, inform the shift supervisor in charge of the floor immediately, and not re-enter until the shift supervisor has assessed the alarm under PR-12 Cold-chain handling and PR-14 Emergency evacuation where required.

4. A manual temperature verification is carried out every shift. The inbound or picking staff assigned to Zone E must check and record the displayed temperature at the start of the morning shift 06:00-14:00 and at the start of the afternoon shift 14:00-22:00, and additionally after any prolonged door opening, alarm or power interruption. Each reading is entered on the Zone E log with date, time, reading and signature.

5. Entry to Zone E is restricted to authorised staff with a task in the zone. Visitors, drivers and contractors may only enter when escorted by the shift supervisor and for a specific reason. The shift supervisor controls access and ensures no person works alone in Zone E without a check-in arrangement.

6. Door discipline is mandatory. Personnel doors and insulated roller doors to Zone E must be kept closed at all times except for immediate entry and exit of persons, pallets and pallet jacks. Doors must not be wedged, blocked open, or held open to stage goods. Any door fault, ice build-up, seal damage or alarm failure must be reported immediately to the shift supervisor and to the maintenance technician.

7. Mandatory warehouse PPE applies in full inside Zone E. Every person must wear a high-visibility vest outermost and class S3 safety footwear at all times, with no exceptions for short entries. In addition, approved cold-zone clothing — insulated jacket, trousers and gloves — must be worn as defined in PR-12 Cold-chain handling. Additional PPE is worn over, never instead of, vest and safety footwear.

8. Exposure must be limited. No person may remain in Zone E longer than the task requires. Staff who feel excessively cold, wet, dizzy or unwell must leave immediately, close the door and report to the shift supervisor. The shift supervisor must rotate tasks to limit continuous cold exposure and ensure warm rest areas are available.

9. Storage discipline in Zone E follows the same general limits. Free block-stacking, where used, is limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height, and rack bays must not exceed their marked capacity. Aisles and pedestrian walkways must be kept clear, and condensation, leaks or damaged packaging must be reported immediately. Damaged chilled goods must be moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling.

10. The shift supervisor reviews the manual temperature log during each shift, investigates any reading outside +2 °C to +6 °C, records corrective action, and hands over any open cold-chain issue at end of shift under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. The maintenance technician logs every repair to refrigeration, doors, seals and alarms.

chapter_title: Chapter 3 - Restricted Zones: Cold, Hazmat and Safe Storage
title: 3.2 Hazmat Cage and Spill Response (Zone F)
text:
## hs.ch03.s2 3.2 Hazmat Cage and Spill Response (Zone F)

1. Zone F is the services and control zone of 600 m2 and contains the only area on site where hazardous materials may be stored: a separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2. The cage is physically enclosed, clearly marked, locked and continuously ventilated. No other location in the hall, yard or office annex is approved for hazmat storage.

2. Hazmat must never sit anywhere else. This prohibition is absolute and applies to receiving in Zone A, bulk storage in Zone B, picking in Zone C, dispatch in Zone D, the cold zone in Zone E, and all other parts of Zone F including quarantine, returns inspection and value-added packing. Goods identified as hazmat on receipt must be moved directly to the cage after inspection and booking.

3. The total quantity in the hazmat cage must never exceed 4,000 kg at any time. The limit applies to the combined weight of all pallets, drums and packages present in the cage, not per bay or per stack. The shift supervisor in charge of the floor must verify the current total before authorising any put-away to the cage.

4. A pallet, load included, may weigh at most 900 kg. On this basis the 4,000 kg cage limit corresponds to at most 4 full-weight pallets in the cage at one time. Lighter pallets are counted by actual weight, not by pallet count, and the 4,000 kg total remains the controlling limit.

5. Storage inside the cage must respect general storage limits in addition to the hazmat limit. Rack bays, where used, must not exceed their marked capacity of 2,700 kg per bay, and free block-stacking is limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height. Aisles, access to spill kits, fire equipment and ventilation openings must be kept clear. Incompatible hazmat types must be segregated inside the cage as directed by safety data sheets and PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response.

6. All hazmat movements are governed by PR-13 and by WMS tasks. Put-away to the cage under PR-02 Put-away to storage and any replenishment or dispatch from the cage may only be carried out by trained staff assigned by the shift supervisor. Forklift, reach truck and electric pallet jack movements must observe the site speed limits of 8 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps.

7. Mandatory PPE of high-visibility vest and class S3 safety footwear applies in full, with additional hazmat PPE as required by PR-13 and the product safety data sheet. Additional PPE is worn over, never instead of, the vest and footwear. No person may enter the cage without authorisation from the shift supervisor and without the required additional protection.

8. Spill response is defined in PR-13 and must be followed immediately on any leak, spill, damaged package or vapour release:
   a) stop work, warn others and secure the area; do not touch the material;
   b) inform the shift supervisor immediately;
   c) ventilate if safe to do so and eliminate ignition sources; do not operate electrical equipment inside the affected area;
   d) contain only if trained, protected and the safety data sheet permits it, using the spill kit at Zone F;
   e) evacuate and follow PR-14 Emergency evacuation if the spill cannot be safely contained or if alarms activate.

9. Every hazmat spill, leak, exposure or near-miss must be reported immediately to the shift supervisor, recorded as an incident and reviewed under the incident reporting process. Damaged hazmat packages must be moved to quarantine inside Zone F the same day where safe to do so, or isolated in place if movement would increase risk, pending assessment under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling and PR-13.

10. The shift supervisor monitors cage quantities, access, housekeeping and spill kit readiness each shift, hands over any open hazmat issue under PR-15 End-of-shift handover, and the maintenance technician logs every repair to ventilation, racking, barriers and containment equipment.

chapter_title: Chapter 3 - Restricted Zones: Cold, Hazmat and Safe Storage
title: 3.3 Racking and Free Stacking Limits
text:
## hs.ch03.s3 3.3 Racking and Free Stacking Limits

1. Safe stacking limits apply to all storage on site, in every zone. No pallet, bay or block stack may exceed its posted weight or height limit, regardless of operational urgency. Overloading is treated as an immediate unsafe condition and must be stopped and reported to the shift supervisor.

2. The high-bay pallet racking in Zone B provides 2,400 pallet positions across 2,200 m2 of bulk storage. Each rack bay is rated at a maximum of 2,700 kg per bay. The rating is marked on the bay and must be observed for the combined weight of all pallets and loads placed in that bay.

3. A pallet, load included, may weigh at most 900 kg. This 900 kg figure is the controlling number for all capacity calculations on site. No inbound pallet above 900 kg may be accepted for put-away without re-palletising to compliant weights.

4. The 900 kg pallet weight determines how many pallets may be placed in a single rack bay. At full weight, a bay rated at 2,700 kg may hold at most three pallets, totalling 2,700 kg. Four full-weight pallets would total 3,600 kg and would overload the bay. Even with lighter pallets, the total in any one bay must never exceed 2,700 kg.

5. The same principle applies in the hazmat cage in Zone F. The cage limit is 4,000 kg total at any time, across its entire 60 m2 ventilated area. At 900 kg per pallet this corresponds to at most four full-weight pallets in the cage. Lighter pallets are assessed by actual scale weight, not pallet count, and the 4,000 kg total remains the absolute limit.

6. Free block-stacking is permitted only where racking is not provided and is limited to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height, including the pallet and load. Both limits apply together; the lower of the two governs. Block stacks must be vertical, stable, on a level floor, and must not lean against racking, barriers, walls or doors.

7. All put-away to racking and to block stacks is directed by WMS tasks under PR-02 Put-away to storage. Operators of the 9 counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t and 5 reach trucks rated at 2.0 t must verify bay availability, check the bay load notice, and confirm pallet weight before placement. Placement must respect aisle discipline of 4.0 m main transport aisles and 3.0 m rack storage aisles.

8. No person may climb racking, modify beams, remove safety pins, braces or load notices, or place goods on damaged racking. Any rack strike, impact, bent upright, damaged beam, loose anchor or missing pin must be reported immediately to the shift supervisor and to the maintenance technician. The affected bay must be off-loaded and cordoned off until inspected and cleared.

9. Racking receives a documented safety inspection every month. The maintenance technician logs every repair to racking, barriers and dock equipment. Damaged goods discovered during put-away, replenishment, picking or inspection must be moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling, and must not be returned to racking or block storage.

10. The shift supervisor in charge of the floor monitors bay loading, block-stack height and cage quantities during each shift, checks that daily truck checks and speed discipline under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation are observed in storage aisles, and hands over any open storage issue, overload risk or racking damage at end of shift under PR-15 End-of-shift handover.

chapter_title: Chapter 4 - Incidents, Damage and Emergency Response
title: 4.1 Incident Reporting and Review
text:
1. Every incident, near-miss and unsafe condition at Harborwick 3PL must be reported immediately, without exception for severity or outcome. This includes any injury or ill health, vehicle contact or near-contact with a person, rack strike or impact, dropped load, spill or leak including in the hazmat cage, temperature alarm in Zone E, fire or evacuation alarm, and any breach of speed, walkway or dock discipline under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse and PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response.

2. The person involved or first observing the event must stop work where safe to do so, warn others in the immediate area, secure the location to prevent further harm, and inform the shift supervisor in charge of the floor immediately. No attempt may be made to continue work, move damaged racking or goods, or re-enter an affected area until cleared.

3. The shift supervisor is responsible for immediate incident response on every shift, Monday to Friday 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00 and any Saturday overtime approved by the Warehouse Manager. On notification the shift supervisor takes control of the floor, secures the area, provides first response including first aid and spill containment where trained and safe, and arranges emergency services where required under PR-14 Emergency evacuation.

4. The shift supervisor decides whether the area can remain in use, must be cordoned off, or requires full evacuation. Affected bays, aisles, dock doors, trucks and equipment must remain out of service and tagged where necessary until the shift supervisor has inspected and cleared them. The maintenance technician is called immediately for any racking damage, barrier damage, truck defect or equipment fault and must log every repair.

5. Every event must be captured in a written incident report on the same shift. The report is started by the involved staff and the shift supervisor together and must record date, time, zone A-F and exact location, persons involved and witnesses, equipment and pallet weights where relevant, a factual description of what happened, immediate action taken, and any photos or WMS task references.

6. Reporting is not delayed for assessment of damage or blame. A near-miss where no injury or damage occurred is reported and recorded in the same way as an injury. Failure to report, late reporting or restarting work without clearance is treated as an unsafe act.

7. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report before it is closed. The review checks facts, identifies immediate and root causes, confirms whether PR-01 to PR-15 were followed, defines corrective actions including retraining, re-authorisation of forklift operators, repair of racking, barriers or levellers, and confirms whether a second count, quarantine under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling or write-off is required.

8. The Warehouse Manager is accountable for the whole site and ensures that supervision, follow-up and close-out are completed. Serious injuries, any incident requiring external emergency response, repeated near-misses, rack collapses and any incident involving the hazmat cage or cold zone are escalated by the shift supervisor to the Warehouse Manager on the same day. Authorisation of a forklift operator is suspended after any incident or unsafe driving observation pending retraining and personal re-authorisation by the Warehouse Manager.
